citation.title: Estimating Average Causal Effects Under General Interference, with Application to a Social Network Experiment

standing_assumptions:
[Population and design: pp. 1914–1915 (PDF pp. 3–4)] Formally, suppose we have a finite population $U$ of units indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$ on which a randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{1, \ldots, M\}$ specifies which of $M$ possible treatment values that unit $i$ receives. An experimental design contains a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ from the $M^N$ different possibilities with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by a given experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$ so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Our analysis below focuses on the case where the design is known in the following sense: $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$ for all $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ is known. [Exposure mapping: p. 1915 (PDF p. 4)] We define an exposure mapping as a function that maps an assignment vector and unit-specific traits to an exposure value: $f : \Omega 	imes \Theta 	o \Delta$, where $	heta_i \in \Theta$ quantifies relevant traits of unit $i$. [Exposures and exposure probabilities: p. 1916 (PDF p. 5)] Define the exposure that unit $i$ receives as $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z}, 	heta_i)$, a random variable with support $\Delta_i \subseteq \Delta$ and for which $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. Note that because $|\Delta| \le |\Omega| 	imes N$, $\Delta$ is a finite set of $K \le |\Omega| 	imes N$ values, such that $\Delta = \{d_1, \ldots, d_K\}$. Then for each unit, $i$, we have a vector of probabilities, $(\pi_i(d_1), \ldots, \pi_i(d_K))' =  oldsymbol{\pi}_i$. [...] We have $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \Omega} p_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k)$. [...] we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$ as the probability of the joint event that both units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposure $d_k$, and we define $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$ as the probability of the joint event that units $i$ and $j$ are subject to exposures $d_k$ and $d_l$, respectively. [Probability matrices: p. 1917 (PDF p. 6)] $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ is an $N 	imes N$ symmetric matrix with individual exposure probabilities, the $\pi_i(d_k)$'s, on the diagonal and joint exposure probabilities, the $\pi_{ij}(d_k)$'s, on the off-diagonals. The nonsymmetric $N 	imes N$ matrix $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$, with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)$, yields all joint probabilities across exposure conditions $k$ and $l$. The zeroes on the diagonal are due to the fact that a unit cannot be subject to multiple exposure conditions at once. [Positivity: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] Suppose all units have nonzero probabilities of being subject to each of the $K$ exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for all $i$ and $k$. [Potential outcomes: p. 1918 (PDF p. 7)] In the most general terms, each $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ can generate a potential outcome for unit $i$. We label the randomization potential outcome of unit $i$ associated with $\mathbf{z}$ as $y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$. These randomization potential outcomes are fixed for all units in the population and do not depend on the value of randomized treatment, $\mathbf{Z}$. CONDITION 1 (Properly specified exposure mapping). For all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = f(\mathbf{z}', 	heta_i)$, $y_i^r(\mathbf{z}) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z}')$. Given Condition 1, each unit $i$ has $|\Delta| = K$ potential outcomes, which we can write in terms of the exposure conditions as $(y_i(d_1), \ldots, y_i(d_K))$, where $y_i(d_k) = y_i^r(\mathbf{z})$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, $k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$, and $\mathbf{z} \in \Omega$ such that $f(\mathbf{z}, 	heta_i) = d_k$. Let $Y_i$ be the observed outcome for unit $i$. CONDITION 2 (Consistent potential outcomes). $Y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) y_i(d_k)$, $ orall i \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$. [p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] Throughout, unless otherwise noted, we will be assuming Conditions 1 and 2. [Estimands: p. 1919 (PDF p. 8)] We seek estimates for all $k$ of $\mu(d_k) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) =  rac{1}{N} y^T(d_k)$, where $y^T(d_k)$ is the total of the potential outcomes under $d_k$. This allows us to define an average causal effect of being in exposure condition $d_k$ as compared to being in condition $d_l$ as $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k) -  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_l)$. [Estimators: pp. 1919–1920 (PDF pp. 8–9)] (1) $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}$. $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) = (1/N)\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) = (1/N^2)\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$. (3) $\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) = \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_l) =  rac{1}{N}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k) - \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]$, which is an estimator of $	au(d_k, d_l) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[y_i(d_k) - y_i(d_l)]$, the average unit-level causal effect of exposure $k$ versus exposure $l$. [Exact probabilities: p. 1920 (PDF p. 9)] from here on our analysis assumes that we are working with $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_k'$ and $\mathbf{I}_k\mathbf{P}\mathbf{I}_l'$ [the exact exposure probabilities; the simulated probabilities $\widehat{\pi}_i(d_k)$ enter only Propositions 3.1 and 4.1]. [Variance and covariance estimators of Section 5, used by several targets: pp. 1921–1924 (PDF pp. 10–13)] Given $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$, the Horvitz–Thompson estimator for $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)]$ is (7) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] = \sum_{i \in U} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)[1 - \pi_i(d_k)] \left[ rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}ight]^2 + \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) 	imes  rac{\pi_{ij}(d_k) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_k)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_k)}$. [p. 1922 (PDF p. 11)] (This notation requires that we define $0/0 = 0$.) [p. 1922] $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_k) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_k)}ight]$, noting that $\widehat{A_2}(d_k) = 0$ if $\pi_{ij}(d_k) > 0$ for all $i, j$. [p. 1923 (PDF p. 12)] For the case where $\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0$ for all $i, j$ such that $i 
e j$, we propose the Horvitz–Thompson-type estimator for the covariance (8) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in U \setminus i} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_l) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] a more general estimator for the covariance (10) $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] = \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U \setminus i : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) > 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k)\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l)}{\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l)}  rac{Y_i}{\pi_i(d_k)}  rac{Y_j}{\pi_j(d_l)} 	imes [\pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) - \pi_i(d_k)\pi_j(d_l)]ight] - \sum_{i \in U}\sum_{j \in \{U : \pi_{ij}(d_k, d_l) = 0\}} \left[ rac{\mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) Y_i^2}{2\pi_i(d_k)} +  rac{\mathbf{I}(D_j = d_l) Y_j^2}{2\pi_j(d_l)}ight]$. [p. 1924] we obtain a conservative variance estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l))$ as (11) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] =  rac{1}{N^2}\{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_k) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)] + \widehat{A_2}(d_l) - 2\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}_A}[\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k), \widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_l)]\}$. [Asymptotic framework and the conditions of Section 6. These are not standing assumptions: they are transcribed here once because several targets invoke them, and a target carries one of them only where its statement names it.] [p. 1924 (PDF p. 13)] Consider a sequence of nested populations indexed by size $N$, $(U_N)$. To define a notion of asymptotic growth, we let $N$ tend to infinity, allowing for the experimental design to be reapplied anew to each $U_N$, subject to the conditions defined below. [p. 1925 (PDF p. 14)] CONDITION 3 (Boundedness of potential outcomes and exposure probabilities). Potential outcomes and exposure probabilities are bounded so that, for all values $i$ and $d_k$, $|y_i(d_k)| \le c_1 < \infty$ and $|1/\pi_i(d_k)| \le c_2 < \infty$. [p. 1925] Define a pairwise dependency indicator $g_{ij}$ such that if $g_{ij} = 0$, then $D_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_j$, else let $g_{ij} = 1$. CONDITION 4 (Restrictions on pairwise dependence). $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = o(N^2)$. otin \Gamma_1$ and $i \in \Gamma_2$, $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_1\}$ and $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_2\}$ are independent. CONDITION 5 (Local dependence). There exists a finite constant $m$ such that, for all $U_N$, $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$. [p. 1926 (PDF p. 15)] CONDITION 6 (Nonzero limiting variance.). $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{	au_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] \xrightarrow{p} c$, where $c > 0$. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] $\mathrm{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}$ are taken over the randomization distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$ with weights $p_{\mathbf{z}}$; the population, the traits $	heta_i$, the exposure mapping and the potential outcomes are fixed. $U \setminus i$ means $U \setminus \{i\}$. Each unit receives exactly one exposure, so $\sum_{k} \mathbf{I}(D_i = d_k) = 1$, $\pi_{ii}(d_k) = \pi_i(d_k)$ and $\pi_{ii}(d_k, d_l) = 0$ for $d_k

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition of the dependency indicator $h_{ij}$, corrected, with Condition 5 and the claim that Condition 5 subsumes Condition 4
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected definition, p. 1925 (PDF p. 14): each of the four printed $\notin$ is replaced by $\in$; nothing else changes.] Define a binary dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ over all pairs $(i, j) \in \{1, 2, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$, where $h_{ij}$ satisfies the following: for any pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2 \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ such that there exists no pair $(i, j)$ with $h_{ij} = 1$ and either (i) $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, (ii) $j \in \Gamma_1$ and $i \in \Gamma_2$, (iii) $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, or (iv) $j \in \Gamma_1$ and $i \in \Gamma_2$, $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_1\}$ and $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_2\}$ are independent. [Equivalent wording given by the validator] Define a symmetric binary dependency indicator $h_{ij}$ such that, for every pair of disjoint sets $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, if $h_{ij} = 0$ for all $i \in \Gamma_1$ and $j \in \Gamma_2$, the random vectors $(D_i)_{i \in \Gamma_1}$ and $(D_j)_{j \in \Gamma_2}$ are independent. [Condition 5, unchanged] CONDITION 5 (Local dependence). There exists a finite constant $m$ such that, for all $U_N$, $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$. [Statements that hold with the corrected definition] (a) With the four replacements, clauses (i) and (iii) coincide and clauses (ii) and (iv) coincide, and the antecedent says exactly that there is no pair $(i, j)$ with $h_{ij} = 1$ having one index in $\Gamma_1$ and the other in $\Gamma_2$, in either order; for symmetric $h$ this is: $h_{ij} = 0$ for all $i \in \Gamma_1$, $j \in \Gamma_2$. (b) If $h$ satisfies the corrected definition, then for $i \ne j$ with $h_{ij} = h_{ji} = 0$ the exposures $D_i$ and $D_j$ are independent. Hence $g_{ij} := 1$ if $i = j$ or $h_{ij} = 1$ or $h_{ji} = 1$, and $g_{ij} := 0$ otherwise, is a pairwise dependency indicator in the sense of p. 1925. (c) [Condition 5 subsumes Condition 4, p. 1926] If in addition $\sum_{j=1}^{N} h_{ij} \le m$ for every $i$, then for this $g$, $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} \le N(2m + 1)$, and $\le N(m + 1)$ when $h$ is symmetric. So along a sequence of populations satisfying Condition 5 with the corrected definition, $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = O(N) = o(N^2)$ and Condition 4 holds.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed definition, Conditions 4 and 5 and the definition of $g_{ij}$ are in the standing assumptions (p. 1925, PDF p. 14). Independence of $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_1\}$ and $\{D_i, i \in \Gamma_2\}$ means independence of the two random vectors of exposures under the randomization distribution; for an empty set the vector is constant.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (b) is the corrected definition applied to the singletons $\Gamma_1 = \{i\}$, $\Gamma_2 = \{j\}$. (c) counts, for each $i$, the index $j = i$, at most $m$ indices with $h_{ij} = 1$ and at most $\sum_i\sum_j h_{ji} \le Nm$ further ordered pairs in total.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: replace all four occurrences of $\notin$ with $\in$; equivalently the symmetric wording quoted above; keep Condition 5's uniform row bound, with either diagonal convention accommodated by a constant adjustment. The validator checked the equivalence in (a) for all 512 binary $3 \times 3$ matrices and all 27 ordered pairs of disjoint subsets. Pairwise independence of nonadjacent units alone is weaker than the corrected definition and is not enough for the central limit theorem (the second example in the note of P013-T5). This is the Condition 5 used by P013-T2.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A.7 (proof of Proposition 6.2), convergence claims of the first and last paragraphs, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements refuted: Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32)] By Proposition 5.6, $\mathrm{E}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] \ge N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$. Thus, by Chebyshev's inequality, $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]] \xrightarrow{p} 0$ is sufficient to establish convergence of $N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$ to a value greater than or equal to $N\,\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]$, which is itself nonzero by Condition 6. [...] Define $t = \frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}} = \frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}} \left(\frac{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}\right)^{1/2}$. Under Conditions 3, 5, and 6, then, by Chen and Shao [(2004), Theorem 2.7], $\frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}}$ is asymptotically $\mathrm{N}(0, 1)$, while $(\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]/\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)])^{1/2}$ converges in probability to a quantity in $(0, 1]$. By Slutsky's theorem, $t$ is asymptotically normal [...]. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $n_0 = 0$ and $n_r = 2^{2^r}$ for integers $r \ge 1$. The population is the positive integers and $U_N = \{1, \ldots, N\}$. Block $r$ consists of the integers $n_{r-1} + 1, \ldots, n_r$. There are two exposures, $d_k = 1$ and $d_l = 0$. The potential outcomes $(y_i(1), y_i(0))$ are $(1, 1)$ for every unit in a block with $r$ odd; in a block with $r$ even the units alternate $(2, 0), (0, 2), (2, 0), \ldots$, starting with $(2, 0)$. For each $N$ the assignments $Z_1, \ldots, Z_N$ are independent with $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \Pr(Z_i = 0) = 1/2$, $D_i = Z_i$, and $Y_i = Z_iy_i(1) + (1 - Z_i)y_i(0)$. Write $\tau_N$, $\widehat{\tau}_N$, $V_N = \mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau}_N]$ and $\widehat{V}_N$ (expression (11)) for the population $U_N$. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] Conditions 1 and 2 hold; Condition 3 holds with $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = 2$; the exposure vectors of any two disjoint sets of units are independent, so $h_{ij} = 1$ for $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise is a genuine dependency graph and Condition 5 holds with $m = 1$; every joint exposure probability of two distinct units is $1/4$. With $R_i = 2Z_i - 1$, $\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N = \frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} R_i$, so $V_N = 4/N$ and $N V_N = 4$ for every $N$: Condition 6 holds with $c = 4$. Also $|\tau_N| \le 2/N$. (b) [The printed estimator.] $\widehat{V}_N = \frac{4}{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Y_i^2$. Let $B_N$ be the set of units $i \le N$ in blocks with $r$ even, $b_N = |B_N|$, $f_N = b_N/N$, and for $i \in B_N$ let $s_i = +1$ if $(y_i(1), y_i(0)) = (2, 0)$ and $s_i = -1$ if it is $(0, 2)$. Then $W_N := N\widehat{V}_N = 4 + 4f_N + \frac{8}{N}\sum_{i \in B_N} s_iR_i$, $\mathrm{E}[W_N] = 4 + 4f_N \ge 4 = N V_N$, and $\mathrm{Var}(W_N) = 64b_N/N^2 \le 64/N \to 0$. (c) [No single limit.] $0 \le f_{n_r} \le n_{r-1}/n_r$ for odd $r$, $0 \le 1 - f_{n_r} \le n_{r-1}/n_r$ for even $r$, and $n_{r-1}/n_r = 2^{-2^{r-1}}$ for $r \ge 2$, which tends to $0$. Hence $W_{n_r} \xrightarrow{p} 4$ along odd $r$ and $W_{n_r} \xrightarrow{p} 8$ along even $r$: $N\widehat{V}_N$ does not converge to a value although $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{V}_N] \to 0$, and $(V_N/\widehat{V}_N)^{1/2} = (4/W_N)^{1/2}$ tends in probability to $1$ along odd $r$ and to $1/\sqrt{2}$ along even $r$, so it does not converge in probability. (d) [The studentized statistic has two subsequential limits.] $Z_N := (\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N)/\sqrt{V_N} = N^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} R_i$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, while $t_N = Z_N(V_N/\widehat{V}_N)^{1/2}$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ along $N = n_r$ with $r$ odd and to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1/2)$ along $N = n_r$ with $r$ even; so $t_N$ has no limit in distribution.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. Here $M = 2$ with treatment values $0, 1$, $K = 2$, $f(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i) = z_i$ and $\Omega = \{0, 1\}^N$ with $p_{\mathbf{z}} = 2^{-N}$. The printed $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ is read as $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ (P013-E012).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $N$: $\mathbf{I}(D_i = 1)y_i(1)/\tfrac12 - \mathbf{I}(D_i = 0)y_i(0)/\tfrac12 = (y_i(1) - y_i(0)) + 2R_i$, since $y_i(1) + y_i(0) = 2$ for every unit; $V_N = 4/N$; the reduction of (7), (10), (11) to $\widehat{V}_N = 4N^{-2}\sum_i Y_i^2$ (all distinct-unit covariance coefficients vanish because the joint probabilities are $1/4$, the $\widehat{A_2}$ terms vanish, and (10) reduces to $-\sum_i Y_i^2$); $Y_i^2 = 1$ for a unit with outcomes $(1, 1)$ and $Y_i^2 = 2 + 2s_iR_i$ for $i \in B_N$; the formulas for $W_N$, $\mathrm{E}[W_N]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(W_N)$ in (b); the bounds on $f_{n_r}$ in (c). Exact values from the validator's enumeration: at $N = 8$, $b_N = 4$, $\tau_N = 0$, $N V_N = 4$, $\mathrm{E}[W_N] = 6$, $\mathrm{Var}(W_N) = 4$. The limits in (c) and (d) then use Chebyshev's inequality, the characteristic function $\cos(u/\sqrt{N})^N \to \exp(-u^2/2)$ of $Z_N$, and Slutsky's theorem on each subsequence.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E007 is rated an error, Minor. The counterexample is to steps of the printed proof, not to the coverage conclusion: in this sequence the coverage of the nominal $1 - \alpha$ interval tends to $1 - \alpha$ along odd-block endpoints and to $2\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{2}) - 1$ along even-block endpoints, so its lower limit is $1 - \alpha$ (P013-T8). The printed “$\mathrm{Var}[\ldots] \xrightarrow{p} 0$” concerns a deterministic sequence and is read as ordinary convergence. The sequence has a genuine dependency graph and joint probabilities bounded away from zero, so it does not depend on P013-E001 or P013-E002.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A.7 (proof of Proposition 6.2), concentration and coverage steps, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected argument replacing the two passages quoted in P013-T7. Changes: convergence of the scaled variance estimator “to a value” becomes concentration around its expectation; the claims that the variance ratio converges in probability and that $t$ has a limiting normal law are deleted; coverage is bounded below in the limit inferior.] [Setting and premises] For each $N$ let $\widehat{\tau}_N$, $\tau_N$ be the estimator and estimand of Proposition 6.2, $V_N = \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_N) > 0$, $\widehat{V}_N = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat{\tau}_N)$ (expression (11)), $v_N = N V_N$ and $W_N = N\widehat{V}_N$. Suppose (1) $v_N \to c > 0$, and $Z_N = (\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N)/\sqrt{V_N}$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$; (2) $\mathrm{E}[W_N] \ge v_N$ for every $N$; (3) $\mathrm{Var}(W_N) \to 0$. [Statement] (a) $W_N - \mathrm{E}[W_N] \xrightarrow{p} 0$. This does not give a limit for $W_N$ unless $\mathrm{E}[W_N]$ converges. (b) For each $0 < \epsilon < 1$ and each $N$, $\Pr(W_N < (1 - \epsilon)v_N) \le \frac{\mathrm{Var}(W_N)}{\epsilon^2 v_N^2}$, which tends to $0$. (c) For each $0 < \alpha < 1$ and $0 < \epsilon < 1$, with $z = z_{1-\alpha/2}$, $\liminf_{N \to \infty} \Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}) \ge 2\Phi(z\sqrt{1 - \epsilon}) - 1$; letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, $\liminf_{N \to \infty} \Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}) \ge 1 - \alpha$. No convergence of $\mathrm{E}[W_N]$, of the ratio $V_N/\widehat{V}_N$, or of $t = (\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N)/\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}$ is asserted. (d) [What recovers the printed limit] If in addition $\mathrm{E}[W_N] \to s$ for a finite $s \ge c$, then $W_N \xrightarrow{p} s$, $(V_N/\widehat{V}_N)^{1/2} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{c/s} \in (0, 1]$, and $t$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, c/s)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Conditions 1–6, expressions (1), (3), (7), (10), (11) and $\widehat{A_2}$ are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function and $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ its $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile. In Proposition 6.2, premise (1) comes from Condition 6 and the central limit theorem cited from Chen and Shao (2004), Theorem 2.7; premise (2) is Proposition 5.6; premise (3) is the bound $\mathrm{Var}[N\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}] = O(N^{-1})$ of Appendix A.7, which needs the added hypothesis of P013-T2.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $N$, with $\mathrm{E}[W_N] \ge v_N > 0$ and $0 < \epsilon < 1$: if $W_N < (1 - \epsilon)v_N$ then $\mathrm{E}[W_N] - W_N > \epsilon v_N$, so by Chebyshev's inequality $\Pr(W_N < (1 - \epsilon)v_N) \le \mathrm{Var}(W_N)/(\epsilon^2 v_N^2)$. On the event $W_N \ge (1 - \epsilon)v_N$, $\widehat{V}_N > 0$ and $\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N/V_N} = \sqrt{W_N/v_N} \ge \sqrt{1 - \epsilon}$, hence $\Pr(|\widehat{\tau}_N - \tau_N| \le z\sqrt{\widehat{V}_N}) \ge \Pr(|Z_N| \le z\sqrt{1 - \epsilon}, W_N \ge (1 - \epsilon)v_N) \ge \Pr(|Z_N| \le z\sqrt{1 - \epsilon}) - \Pr(W_N < (1 - \epsilon)v_N)$. The corrected algebraic identity $t = Z_N (V_N/\widehat{V}_N)^{1/2}$ holds whenever $V_N > 0$ and $\widehat{V}_N > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: replace convergence to a value with concentration around $\mathrm{E}[N\widehat{V}_N]$; delete the single variance-ratio and studentized-normal limit claims; use the one-sided Chebyshev inequality in (b) and the true-variance central limit theorem to show that the lower limit of coverage is at least $1 - \alpha$. No independence of $Z_N$ and $W_N$ is used. This is an abstract statement about sequences of random variables and is the last step of P013-T2, which replaces premise (3) by the weaker lower-tail condition (L); the counterexample P013-T7 satisfies premises (1)–(3). On the event $\widehat{V}_N < 0$ any convention for the interval may be used, since that event is contained in $\{W_N < (1 - \epsilon)v_N\}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Centering and coverage targets in Appendix A.6, Proposition 6.2, Appendix A.7 and the sentence before Proposition 4.1, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [The paper defines the population quantities $\mu(d_k)$, $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ and $y^T(d_k)$ (p. 1919) and their estimators $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)$, $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ and $\widehat{y^T_{HT}}(d_k)$. As printed, $\mu_{HT}(d_k)$ and $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ appear without hats as centering or coverage targets, and $\widehat{y^T}(d_k)$ appears as the quantity being estimated; none of these is defined. Corrected, the targets are the population quantities.] (i) [Appendix A.6, p. 1942 (PDF p. 31), corrected] Consistency of $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)$ for $\mu(d_k)$ is therefore ensured when $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij} = o(N^2)$, as this implies that $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu(d_k) \xrightarrow{p} 0$. Consistency of $\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)$ for $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ follows by Slutsky's theorem. [Formal content: under Conditions 1 and 2, and under Conditions 3 and 4 along the sequence of populations of Section 6, $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu(d_k) \xrightarrow{p} 0$ as $N \to \infty$.] (ii) [Proposition 6.2, p. 1926 (PDF p. 15), corrected final clause] [...] will tend to cover $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ at least $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ of the time for large $N$. [The full corrected proposition is P013-T2.] (iii) [Appendix A.7, p. 1943 (PDF p. 32), corrected display] Define $t = \frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}} = \frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}} \left(\frac{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}\right)^{1/2}$, and in the two sentences that follow the standardized quantity is $\frac{\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l) - \tau(d_k, d_l)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)]}}$ and the intervals cover $\tau(d_k, d_l)$. [Formal content: the displayed equality holds whenever $\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] > 0$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\widehat{\tau_{HT}}(d_k, d_l)] > 0$.] (iv) [p. 1920 (PDF p. 9), corrected sentence] Following Fattorini (2006), the following proposition provides guidance on choosing $R$ in terms of a bound on the relative bias for estimating $y^T(d_k)$. [The corrected proposition is P013-T4.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mu(d_k)$, $\tau(d_k, d_l)$, $y^T(d_k)$, the estimators (1) and (3), Conditions 3 and 4, the indicator $g_{ij}$ and expression (11) are in the standing assumptions. [As printed] p. 1942: “as this implies that $\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu_{HT}(d_k) \xrightarrow{p} 0$”; p. 1926: “will tend to cover $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$”; p. 1943: $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ in both numerators of the display defining $t$, in the standardized quantity of the next sentence and in the final coverage sentence; p. 1920: “a bound on the relative bias for estimating $\widehat{y^T}(d_k)$”.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For (i), from Appendix A.6 (p. 1942), for each fixed $N$: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)] = \mu(d_k)$ (Lemma 4.1); Condition 3 implies $|y_i(d_k)|/\pi_i(d_k) \le c_3 < \infty$ with $c_3 = c_1c_2$; substituting in expression (2), $N^2\,\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k)) \le c_3^2N + c_3^2\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} g_{ij}$; and by Chebyshev's inequality $\Pr(|\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k) - \mu(d_k)| > \epsilon) \le \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mu_{HT}}(d_k))/\epsilon^2$ for $\epsilon > 0$. For (iii): the identity is algebra on positive reals.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E012 is rated an error, Minor: misprinted symbols in formulas (five unhatted $\tau_{HT}$, one on p. 1926 and four on p. 1943; one unhatted $\mu_{HT}$ on p. 1942; one stray hat on p. 1920), which a reader corrects from the definitions nearby. Sol's smallest repair: replace the five unhatted $\tau_{HT}(d_k, d_l)$ targets by $\tau(d_k, d_l)$ and the unhatted $\mu_{HT}(d_k)$ target in A.6 by $\mu(d_k)$; in the sentence before Proposition 4.1 replace $\widehat{y^T}(d_k)$ by $y^T(d_k)$; retain hats and HT subscripts on estimators. The notation repair does not by itself repair the proofs: (ii) and (iii) are subject to P013-E001 and P013-E007. Part (i) is the step on which Proposition 6.1 (P013-T19) rests; the finding also touches P013-H4 through (ii) and (iii).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 2, WLS rows $\tau(d_{101}, d_{000})$ and $\tau(d_{111}, d_{000})$: estimate and 95% CI, corrected claim
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed entries: Table 2, p. 1936 (PDF p. 25), columns Estimator, Estimand, Estimate, S.E., 95% CI] WLS, $\tau(d_{101}, d_{000})$: 0.295, 0.124, $(0.050, 0.536)$. WLS, $\tau(d_{111}, d_{000})$: 0.306, 0.049, $(0.212, 0.404)$. [Table note] S.E. = Estimated standard error; CI = Normal approximation confidence interval. [Corrected claim, from the validator] In each of these two rows the printed estimate and the printed interval endpoints cannot arise from a symmetric interval about that estimate, even allowing three-decimal rounding of every entry. At least one of the estimate and the two endpoints is wrong in each row; the replacement entries cannot be determined from the published table. [Formal content] Say that a real number $x$ displays as the three-decimal number $p$ if $p - \tfrac{1}{2000} \le x \le p + \tfrac{1}{2000}$ (closed bins, so every round-to-nearest tie rule is allowed). (a) For all real $e, s, z$: $(e - zs) + (e + zs) = 2e$. (b) There are no real numbers $e, L, U$ with $L + U = 2e$ such that $e$ displays as $0.295$, $L$ displays as $0.050$ and $U$ displays as $0.536$. (c) There are no real numbers $e, L, U$ with $L + U = 2e$ such that $e$ displays as $0.306$, $L$ displays as $0.212$ and $U$ displays as $0.404$. Consequently, for no estimate $e$, standard error $s$ and critical value $z$ do $e$, $e - zs$ and $e + zs$ display as the printed estimate and endpoints of either row.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: A normal approximation confidence interval with estimate $e$, standard error $s$ and critical value $z$ has endpoints $L = e - zs$ and $U = e + zs$. No other object of the paper is needed; the statement concerns the printed numbers only.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Row $\tau(d_{101}, d_{000})$: the estimate requires $0.2945 \le e \le 0.2955$, while the endpoints require $0.2925 \le (L + U)/2 \le 0.2935$. Row $\tau(d_{111}, d_{000})$: the estimate requires $0.3055 \le e \le 0.3065$, while the endpoints require $0.3075 \le (L + U)/2 \le 0.3085$. In each row the two closed intervals are disjoint, with a gap of exactly $1/1000$.
canonical_claim.note: P013-E008 is rated an error, Minor. It is a finding about reported numbers, included because its entire content is an exact arithmetic impossibility; the “corrected statement” is the validator's corrected text, since the corrected table entries are not recoverable from the paper. The validator already holds a Lean certificate (validate/P013-E008/v1/artifact/check.lean, with lean-output.txt), which the formalizer may restate in the project namespace. Not part of the error: the WLS row $\tau(d_{001}, d_{000})$, printed 0.056, 0.066, $(-0.072, 0.186)$, is consistent, but only at a rounding boundary ($e = 113/2000$, $L = -145/2000$, $U = 371/2000$ are forced, and $s = 129/1960$ with $z = 49/25$ is a witness). When this target was fixed no estimate had been recomputed from data; a later reconstruction on the public data is described in the record of P013-E008 and does not change the arithmetic stated here.
